newsitem.title: GERMANY: Berliners hesitant to give up marks for euro trial.
newsitem.headline: Berliners hesitant to give up marks for euro trial.

text.p: The German capital's first chance to shop with Europe's planned single currency got off to a slow start on Friday as consumers seemed reluctant to trade their beloved deutschemarks -- even for a test run.

As retailers, banks and the European Commission lauched a 10-day trial programme called "The Euro is Rolling" in Berlin, most of the over 50 participating shops and restaurants reported sluggish business with the currency.

"We haven't had a single euro purchase today," said Christine Volkhardt, manager of a discount shoe store with rows of 30 euro pumps on display. "Most of our customers find the whole idea of giving up the mark a terrible idea."

Many Germans fear that the euro will be a weaker currency than the deutschemark, a symbol of post-war economic prosperity and stability. Some feel the price of introducing the currency is already too high as Germany has had to cut government spending to meet convergence criteria for monetary union.
"I'm certainly not looking forward to giving up the mark," said Iselotta Lau, 67, buying a frying pan at the Kaufhof am Alex department store's "Euro Days" stand and paying in marks.
"I must say I am sceptical. I'm from east Germany and we've traded our currency three times now in my lifetime. I have a feeling this time it is not in our interest."
For just over a week, Berliners have been able to exchange their currency at hundreds of local banks at a rate of two marks to one euro. Friday was the first day they had the chance to spend them.

Stores tried to bring people round to the idea of using the euro by hanging promotional posters and European flags in their windows, but most shopkeepers had to wait hours to witness their first euro purchases.

This is not the first time Germans have had the chance to try out the new currency. Last October, a similar scheme in the Black Forest town of Waldkirch was foiled by collectors who were more interested in keeping the coins than spending them.

For this reason, organisers in Berlin have issued special coins worth 1.5 euros (three marks), 2.5 euros (five marks) and 10 euro notes (20 marks). The silver and bronze coins dwarf the mark in size, at about 40 mm in diameter.

These odd-value coins, featuring the city's landmark Brandenburg Gate on one side and the European continent on the other, will become void when the real euro is launched and organisers hope this will deter collectors.

If European economic and monetary union (EMU) moves forward as planned, citizens in participating countries will see their national currency phased out between January and July 2002 and replaced with the euro.

Euro business proved a bit brisker at a Berlin McDonald's where the fast food chain was offering four "Euro Vision" menus including a hamburger, a medium-sized bag of french fries, a medium-sized drink and an ice cream for four euros a piece.

"We've had at least five or six customers using euros since lunch started a few hours ago," franchise assistant manager Sabrine Graetz said. "So far it is running smoothly with the cash registers too. We've set up a separate one just for euro customers."
Most locations accepting euros have also divided their tills to expedite bookkeeping. Consumers can receive marks or euros or a combination of the two as change.

A spring festival opposite the Berlin city hall starting on Friday afternoon is also part of the trial programme, with euros valid as legal tender at all stands. Live bands will entertain the crowds and visitors can enjoy a glass of beer for 2.5 euros and a sausage for 1.5 euros.
But even those manning its tents seemed doubtful the event would be a success.

"It is going to be a pain getting used to these things, both for us and for the customers," Hannelore Grosch, 53, said holding up a euro coin as she set up a sandwich stand. "But I suppose we had better just get used to it."
